Action: Complete 'Operational Readiness Review' (ORR)
What it means: Complete a checklist of activities to consider when building a service
Why does this exist:
It's an ITIL* process which other organisations use. It started in 2016 and has accumulated over time. 

It is seen as something that will help people deliver good services. Parts of the ORR are also 'must haves', like ORR item 29 on meeting WCAG 2.2 AA guidelines.  

*ITIL is a widely used framework of best practices for IT Service Management.
Conditions:
Universal - any digital, data, technology service:
- new service
- major change
- decommissioning service
What needs to happen:
'- Team finds out about Steve/ORR and engages with Steve (this varies but typically in alpha)
- Steve guides people through the ORR, he goes through it line by line to talk about what people need to do
- Team fills out ORR and sends it to Steve
Standards applicable: Related to standards but not under a standard
Systems:
- ORR spreadsheet 
- Email inbox and Teams messages
- ORR tracker
Guidance: No written guidance, Steve Goff provides guidance
Pain points:
- Reliance on people and manual processes, Steve is a single point of failure 
- People don't find out about the ORR at the right point 
- People don't have budget for compliance activities 
- Compliance is inconsistent 
- Data and systems are not updated or interoperable
Opportunities:
- ORR currently being looked at for improvements
- A 'front door' for assurance that tells you what you need to do

Action: Complete or update 'Service Health Check App' (SHCA)
What it means: A tool to declare compliance to DfE standards and policies on a yearly basis.
Why does this exist: This came out of audit in April 2023 which found DfE doesn't have a mechanism to view the compliance landscape of their services and for teams to declare compliance. SHCA aims to do this. The standards in it are based on things established in the Standards Forum.
Conditions:
For 'genuine' services (ones that DfE create to deliver things): 
- transactional 
- has users 
- an interface
What needs to happen:
'- Once a service gets a service offering, it will get pulled into SHCA 
- Steve looks at what has been registered on CMDB in the last 7 days
- Steve chases people to complete it (if they haven't already)
- Delivery team goes on SHCA intranet page to find link and guidance  
- Delivery team reports on whether they are meeting the conditions against their service(s) and, if not, what activity is required to achieve each standard  
- Steve is able to check compliance against each standard for a service
- Delivery team is notified yearly to update their entry
Standards applicable: Related to standards but not under a standard
Guidance: Intranet page for Service Health Check Hub
Pain points:
'- Manual reminders for people to fill it out
- People don't find out at the right point 
- Data and systems not updated (e.g. if names of team members go out of date, Steve has to run around to find out who is responsible) 
- Data and systems not connection (e.g. believe there is duplication between the ORR and SHCA)

Action: Get help with DDT tasks and projects ('Demand' process)
What it means: Review of requests from across DfE for DDT time, knowledge and expertise, usually with a view to developing a solution to a problem, or augmenting an existing service.
Why does this exist: Centralised way into DDT for people who don't have ways into DDT. Demand can signpost people to the right place.
What needs to happen:
Teams complete the DDT request form.
They will need to provide:
- a clear description of the problem and its impact
- what kind of help they are seeking. For example, options appraisal or planning advice
- timescales and confirmed funding
- work already done. For example, research, options considered, guidance reviewed
The team will review the demand request and take it through the triage process if there is merit to it.
Systems: MS Form, SharePoint List, Power BI
Guidance: Get help with DDT tasks and projects
[Delete?] Metrics:
Demand measures are tracked on Power BI:
- Number received
- Days to assignment/close
- Status
- Indicator (strategic tags)
- Division assigned
etc
[Delete] Who else is involved: Sam Rye,Lou Clarke,DDT business partners,DDT colleagues
[Unsure?] Assurance point:
Informal: Weekly Demand Review
Formal: High Level Triage and Delivery Triage
Pain points: Quality of demand submission, DDT colleague understanding of Demand's existence, contact tracing
Opportunities: Aim is to move onto COMPASS for stratgic overview of all demand and smooth handoffs into work items
Any other notes:
Work is initiated through a request process, assessed and prioritised through governance, then allocated to delivery teams who implement the agreed solution.
 
Key objectives:
Provide a single, transparent entry point for DDT service requests​

Triage and assess demand for feasibility, alignment, and urgency​

Route requests to appropriate governance boards or delivery teams​

Maintain visibility of pipeline and demand trends​

Support strategic prioritisation and resource planning​

Action: Design and run board
What it means: To check how a service is being designed and run. This helps track whether DfE services are being designed correctly.

Action: Delivery board
What it means: To check how a service is being run. To evaluate risk.
What needs to happen: - G6s/G7s with oversight of an area attend the board meeting.

Action: The DfE security.txt file needs to be accessible from active DfE websites to ensure vulnerabilities can be quickly reported via the HMG-mandated VdP. The file MUST be accessible without authentication and implemented on all domains resolvable from the public Internet
What it means: Every public-facing DfE website must publish a security.txt file so that security researchers can easily find out how to report vulnerabilities to the Department for Education through the government's Vulnerability Disclosure Programme (VdP)
Why does this exist:
Without a clear reporting mechanism, a reported may:
- Not know who to contact.
- Send reports to a generic inbox that nobody monitors.
- Give up reporting the issue.
- Publicly disclose the vulnerability instead of reporting it responsibly.
Conditions: When using a repository
What needs to happen: The file must be accessible without authentication and implemented on all domains that can be reached by the public internet

Action: GitHub Repositories must be tagged to clearly identify service, division and directorate.
What it means: Naming and labelling on GitHub repositories is important so that in the even of a Cyber incident the right person or team can be found quickly
Why does this exist: Ensures vulnerabilities and other security incidents can be quickly routed to the correct owner when speed and accuracy is of the essence to prevent a serious cyber incident occurring.
Conditions: When using a repository
What needs to happen: Repositories must be labelled with the service, division and directorate
Guidance:
Naming things - DfE Technical Guidance

Storing source code - DfE Technical Guidance

Action: Must use GitHub for any new projects. Existing projects should have migration plans developed asap.
What it means:
Any projects using something other than GitHub 
should have migration plans in place and new projects can only use GitHub for source code repository and development platform
Why does this exist: Enables security measures to be designed once and re-used many times, otherwise all teams and projects are required to duplicate effort, and any errors introduce security risk.
Conditions: When using a repository/development platform
What needs to happen: All new project build using GitHub, all existing project have migration plans to move to GitHub asap
Any other notes: Are Azure DevOps Pipelines still an approved service?

Action: Secrets (API keys, passwords, connection strings, certificates) MUST NOT be committed to Git repositories or baked into container images because this prevents immediate compromise of systems and data.
What it means: Never store sensitive credentials in source code repositories or inside container images. Store them in a secure secrets-management solution instead.
Why does this exist: Leaked secrets are exploited in real-time and can enable direct attacker access to our systems and data.
Conditions: When using a repository
What needs to happen: Application secrets should not be stored in Git repositories or container images
Guidance:
https://technical-guidance.education.gov.uk/infrastructure/security/managing-secrets/

Github actions - DfE Technical Guidance

Azure CIP - DfE Technical Guidance

Disaster recovery - DfE Technical Guidance

Action: Dependency scanning (SCA) MUST be implemented in build pipelines to detect known vulnerabilities in third-party libraries, and critical vulnerabilities MUST break the build to prevent deployment of compromised code.
What it means: Your CI/CD pipeline must automatically scan all third-party packages and libraries for known security vulnerabilities. If a critical vulnerability is found, the deployment must be stopped until it is fixed or formally approved as an exception.
Why does this exist:
Modern attacks often exploit weaknesses in third-party libraries rather than vulnerabilities in code written by our developers.
Most applications rely on hundreds or thousands of open-source packages. If  one of those packages contains a known critical vulnerability, an attacker may be able to compromise an entire application.
Conditions: When using a repository
What needs to happen: Add dependency scanning to the CI/CD pipeline. Define the vulnerability thresholds so the pipeline breaks when the threshold is overwhelmed and create a remediation process
Any other notes: A CI/CD pipeline is an automated process that helps developers build, test, and deploy software changes quickly and safely. CI - Continuous Integration and CD - Continuous Delivery merging code and the automated process for preparing for release

Action: Secret scanning MUST be enabled in the repository to ensure proactive detection and remediation of accidental secret exposure.
What it means: Your code repository must automatically scan for passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates, and other secrets so that accidental exposures are detected and fixed quickly.
Why does this exist:
Developers sometimes accidentally commit secrets to Git repositories. Once committed, the secret becomes part of the Git history and may be exposed to
- Other developers
- Contractors
- Automated repository scanners
- Attackers if the repository is public or compromised
Secret scanning helps catch these mistakes before they become security incidents. Leaked secrets are exploited in real-time and can enable direct attacker access to our systems and data.
Conditions: When using a repository
What needs to happen: Put automated detection in place so it is found and remediated before it can be abused.
Any other notes:
Secret scanning tools examine repository contents and look for patterns that resemble credentials.
For example, they can identify:
- Azure keys
- GitHub tokens
- AWS access keys
- Connection strings
- Private keys
- Certificates
- Hardcoded passwords

Action: All infrastructure and digital services MUST be registered and identifiable, and all cloud resources MUST have Owner, CostCenter, and Env tags because this prevents the existence of unsecured, orphaned infrastructure.
What it means: Every system, service, server, database, application, storage account, and cloud resource must be known, recorded, and clearly owned by someone. Cloud resources must also be tagged so they can be identified, managed, secured, and costed correctly.
Why does this exist: Because this prevents the existence of unsecured infrastructure where it is unclear as to who owns it (orphaned resource). We cannot secure what we do not know exists. Orphaned infrastructure is a primary attack vector.
Conditions: Cloud Environments
What needs to happen: Resources shouldn't exist in the cloud that nobody owns, nobody pays for, and nobody is responsible for securing
[Unsure?] Assurance point: If it isn't tagged, the central security function reserves the right to decommission it after a 14-day warning.

Action: All infrastructure and cloud services MUST be securely configured to meet the CIS IG1 baseline/benchmark because this closes known security gaps that hackers actively exploit.
What it means: All servers, cloud resources, platforms, and services must be configured according to the CIS IG1 security baseline so they are protected against common and well-known attacks.
Why does this exist:
Most successful attacks don't rely on sophisticated hacking.
Instead, attackers often exploit:
- Default settings
- Excessive permissions
- Open ports
- Missing encryption
- Poor configurations
Conditions: Configuration Management on platforms, cloud resource and servers
What needs to happen: Teams should build against the approved standard. Don't rely on vendor defaults. Configure every server, cloud resource, and platform according to recognised security standards (CIS IG1) and continuously check that those settings remain in place.

Action: All SaaS/Software MUST be registered in the CMDB to ensure a complete and auditable inventory of digital assets.
What it means: Every software application or SaaS service used by the organisation must be formally recorded in the CMDB (Configuration Management Database) so there is a complete record of what software exists
Why does this exist: We cannot secure what we do not know exists. SaaS is easy to lose track of because it can be bought and used without infrastructure being deployed internally
Conditions: When a product or team purchase a SaaS product
What needs to happen: If a team procures a SaaS product they should use the create a service offering form in Service Now to register the product in the CMDB
Any other notes: Software as a Service (SaaS) is software that is hosted and managed by a third-party provider and accessed over the internet, rather than being installed and operated by our own organisation

Action: All foundation systems MUST meet phase 1 mandated security controls by March 31st 2026 to ensure critical protection against common attacks.
What it means: The organisation has identified a minimum set of essential security controls. Any critical foundational platform must have those controls in place by 31 March 2026, because those controls provide protection against the most common cyber attacks.
Why does this exist:
The purpose is to implement the most important security controls first, reducing risks from common threats such as:
- Phishing
- Credential theft
- Unpatched vulnerabilities
- Misconfigured cloud resources
- Excessive privileges
- Ransomware
Any other notes: What are our foundation systems? What are the controls?

Action: All new services MUST comply with the 10 principles of Secure by Design to ensure security is built-in from the outset.
What it means: When creating a new service, security must be considered from the beginning of the design process, rather than being added later as an afterthought.
Why does this exist: Don't build a service first and worry about security later. Design and build security into the service from day one, following the Secure by Design principles.
Conditions: When building services and making major changes
What needs to happen: Follow Secure by design principles and use the self assessment tracker to monitor progress
Systems: All products and services built in house
Guidance:
https://technical-guidance.education.gov.uk/principles/secure-by-design-principles/

Secure by Design - UK Government Security - Beta

Secure by Design Principles - UK Government Security - Beta

Action: All security tooling procurement MUST be agreed with CISD to ensure consistency, prevent duplication, and avoid unnecessary spend.
What it means: Teams cannot independently buy, subscribe to, or implement security tools without first getting agreement from CISD.
Why does this exist: The organisation wants a single view and governance process for security tooling.
Conditions: If a team believe they need security tooling they should consult with CISD before procuring any tools/software

Action:
Any externally accessible system that:
- Handle sensitive or business‑critical data
- Provide authentication or user accounts
- Connect into internal networks
- Offer custom functionality (web apps, APIs, integrations)
- Could cause material impact if compromised
MUST undergo annual penetration testing against the live production version. Above a threshold this must be an external IT Healthcheck.
What it means: If a system is exposed to the internet and is important enough to pose a security or business risk, it must be tested by security specialists at least once a year to identify vulnerabilities that automated scanning might miss.
Why does this exist: Penetration testing provides assurance that real attackers cannot easily exploit the service.
Conditions: A service or webpage externally accessible and handles sensitive or business critical data (pupil data, financial information, staff data etc), provides authentication or user accounts (login portals, admin portals, identity services etc). If the service connects to internal networks and could cause material impact if compromised
What needs to happen: Penetration testing and IT Health Check
Systems: Service Health Check app and any services who meets the condition criteria

Action: All new services REQUIRE a Security Design Review to ensure security flaws are identified and fixed in the cheapest and easiest stage of the lifecycle.
What it means: Before a new service is built or launched, it must undergo a Security Design Review to identify and address security weaknesses early, when they are easier and less expensive to fix.
Why does this exist: It is much cheaper and safer to identify issues early rather than discovering the problem after the application has gone live and exposed sensitive data.
Conditions: During the design phase of the project a security design review is required
What needs to happen: Security Design review

Action: GovAssure is mandatory if identified as in-scope to ensure compliance with a statutory obligation.
What it means: If your system or service has been identified as being within the scope of GovAssure, then participating in the GovAssure process is not optional. It is a mandatory requirement because it supports a legal or government policy obligation.
Why does this exist: GovAssure is the UK Government's cyber security assurance scheme. It assesses critical government systems against the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) to measure cyber security and resilience.

Action: Third-party tools and integrations (including SaaS) MUST undergo a Vendor Security Assessment before they can be used to prevent breaches via vulnerable suppliers.
What it means: Before a team can use a new supplier, SaaS product, API, integration, or security tool, the supplier's security controls must be assessed and approved.
Why does this exist: The purpose is to avoid introducing security risks through external vendors.

Action: Service Owners MUST own their risk, and risks above tolerance REQUIRE formal consultation with the CISO before acceptance to ensure senior leadership accountability.
What it means: The person responsible for a service is responsible for the risks associated with that service. If a risk is considered too high (above the organisation's risk tolerance), they cannot simply accept it on their own and must consult the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) before deciding to proceed.
Why does this exist:
This control exists because the people closest to a service are often the ones making risk decisions, but the consequences of a poor decision can affect the whole organisation.
Without this rule, it's easy for teams to make local decisions that create enterprise-wide security risk.
Conditions: Where a cyber/security risk is above our tolerance the CISO must be consulted before the risk is accepted (no action planned to address the risk/breach)
What needs to happen: CISO needs to be consulted as a part of the decision making about the risk acceptance

Action: Services MUST undergo mandatory assurance thru DSAM to ensure critical risks are detected and managed effectively.
What it means: Before a service can proceed through key stages of its lifecycle it must go through the DSAM assurance process so that significant risks are identified, assessed, and addressed.
Why does this exist:
Without assurance, teams may unintentionally introduce:
- Security vulnerabilities
- Unsupported technologies
- Compliance issues
- Single points of failure
- Poor operational processes
A formal assurance process provides an independent review and challenge before those issues affect production services.

Action: All systems MUST comply with the requirements stipulated in our Continuous Assurance platform to ensure a minimum baseline of security hardening is applied.
What it means: Every system must meet the security requirements and checks defined by the organisation's Continuous Assurance platform. The platform is used to continuously verify that systems meet a minimum security standard and remain securely configured over time
Why does this exist: The platform continuously checks that a minimum set of security hardening controls remain in place, helping to detect configuration weaknesses and compliance issues before they become security incidents.
Any other notes: All systems is quite clear but what about legacy systems, on-premise systems, SaaS and supplier hosted solutions are they included?

Action: Management interfaces (RDP, SSH, SMB, SQL) MUST NOT be exposed directly to the public internet because this is the fastest way to suffer a critical ransomware event.
What it means: Do not allow administrative access to systems directly from the internet. Management services such as RDP, SSH, SMB, and SQL should only be accessible through secure, controlled routes
Why does this exist: Attackers constantly scan the internet looking for exposed management services. Administrative services should never be directly reachable from the internet. They must be protected behind secure access mechanisms
Conditions: Services that utilise RDP, SSH, SMB or SQL and similar
Any other notes: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol), allows remote log in to Windows servers. SSH (Secure Shell) remotely manage Linux servers. SMB (Server Message Block) file sharing and administration. SQL ports direct administration of databases

Action: Public Web Applications MUST sit behind a Web Application Firewall (WAF) in Blocking Mode to stop common automated attacks.
What it means: Any website or web application accessible from the internet must be protected by a Web Application Firewall (WAF), and the WAF must be actively blocking malicious traffic rather than just monitoring it.
Why does this exist:
Many attacks are:
- Automated
- Opportunistic
- Well known
Attackers don't necessarily target DfE specifically.
Instead, they scan the internet looking for vulnerable applications. A WAF provides an additional layer of defence
Conditions: All public web applications
What needs to happen: A Web Applicational Firewall must be implemented

Action: Production environments MUST NOT communicate with Non-Production environments (Segmentation) to prevent a test environment compromise from spreading to live systems.
What it means: Production systems should be isolated from development, test, and UAT environments. A compromise in a non-production environment should not provide a path into live production systems.
Why does this exist:
Non-production environments are often less secure than production because they may have:
- Weaker access controls
- Shared accounts
- Less monitoring
- Experimental code
- Temporary configurations
Attackers know this.
Conditions: Any applicable in house built service
What needs to happen: Keep Production and Non-Production environments separate. If a development or test system is compromised, the attacker should not be able to use it as a stepping stone into live production services or data.

Action: "Default Encryption" policies MUST be enabled on all Storage Accounts/S3/Blob storage to ensure sensitive data is not accidentally stored without protection.
What it means: Encryption must be turned on by default for all cloud storage services so that any data saved there is automatically protected, even if someone forgets to configure encryption manually.
Why does this exist: Its a security control that reduces the impact of a beach and protects against misconfigured storage, unauthorised access, insider threats and cloud account compromise
Conditions:
This obligation is relevant if your service:
- Stores files, documents, backups, logs, or databases in cloud storage.
- Uses Azure Storage Accounts, Blob Storage, AWS S3, or similar services.
- Handles personal, sensitive, financial, or business-critical data.
Cloud storage services:
Blob Storage - Azure
S3 buckets - AWS (Amazon web services) and similar cloud storage solutions
What needs to happen: All cloud storage services must have encryption enabled by default so that any data stored within them is automatically protected from unauthorised access.

Action: All data repositories (S3, Blob, SQL, SharePoint) MUST be classified to ensure effective data defence.
What it means: Every place where data is stored must have its data classified (labelled according to its sensitivity and importance) so that the correct security controls can be applied.
Why does this exist: Because you can't apply the right security controls if you don't know what data you're protecting.
Conditions: Every database, storage account, SharePoint site, or data store
What needs to happen: Every database, storage account, SharePoint site, or data store must be labelled according to the sensitivity of the data it contains. This allows the organisation to apply the correct level of protection and ensures sensitive data receives stronger security controls than low-risk information.

Action: DLP controls MUST be implemented on email, collaboration tools, and corporate endpoints to prevent the unauthorized transmission of high-risk sensitive data.
What it means: The organisation must have controls (DLP - Data Loss Prevention) in place to detect and stop people from accidentally or deliberately sending sensitive information outside the organisation through email, Teams/SharePoint, or company devices.
Why does this exist:
Most data breaches don't involve sophisticated hackers.
Many occur because of accidental disclosure, unauthorised sharing, and insider activity
Conditions: Email, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, or corporate devices.
What needs to happen: Implement controls that can detect and stop sensitive information leaving the organisation through email, Teams/SharePoint/OneDrive, or corporate devices.

Action: Sensitive data MUST be encrypted At Rest (using managed keys) and In Transit (using TLS 1.2+) to ensure data is protected even if communications are intercepted or storage is compromised.
What it means: Any sensitive data must be encrypted both when it is stored and when it is being transmitted between systems, so that even if someone gains access to the storage or intercepts the communication, they cannot easily read the data.
Why does this exist: To ensure data is protected even if communications are intercepted or storage is compromised
Conditions: Any system that stores, processes or transmits sensitive data
What needs to happen: Sensitive data must be encrypted whenever it is stored and whenever it is transmitted. Use the platform's managed encryption capabilities and modern TLS (1.2 or higher) so that data remains protected if storage systems are compromised or network traffic is intercepted.
Any other notes: Managed keys are like Azure Key Vault or can be managed by the cloud platform. TLS 1.2 is the technology behind HTTPS, TLS stands for Transport Layer Security

Action: Real PII MUST NEVER be used in Non-Prod/Test environments; synthetic or anonymised data MUST be used instead because anonymisation scripts are unreliable and real data causes major data breaches.
What it means: You must not copy real personal data into development, test, UAT, or training environments. Instead, use fake (synthetic) data or properly anonymised data
Why does this exist: Production environments have strict access controls, monitoring, security reviews and limited admin access, but test environments have wider access, temporary configurations so having PII in these environments creates unneccessary risk
Conditions: All test and pre-production environments
What needs to happen: Test with fake data instead. If a test environment is compromised, no real individual should be affected.

Action: All cloud-hosted compute instances and corporate devices MUST run an approved EDR tool with 24/7 monitoring and alerting to the central SoC to ensure detection and stop hackers who bypass initial defences.
What it means: Every cloud server and company-managed device must have an approved Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) security tool installed, and that tool must be continuously monitored by the Security Operations Centre (SOC) so that attacks can be detected and stopped quickly.
Why does this exist: Organisations assume that, despite firewalls, secure passwords, email filtering, and other protections, an attacker may still manage to get onto a device or server. EDR is there to detect and respond when that happens.
Conditions: Applies to all company devices and any cloud servers
What needs to happen: All company devices and cloud servers must have approved security monitoring software installed and connected to the security operations team so cyber attacks can be detected and stopped as quickly as possible.
Any other notes: EDR is End-point detection and response which is an advanced security software that monitors devices for suspicious activity, malware and ransomware, investigates security incidents and unusual behaviour. SOC is the Security Operations Centre the team responsible for monitoring and responding to cyber threats.

Action: "Team" passwords MUST be prohibited because they make accountability impossible and are easy to steal.
What it means: Shared passwords used by multiple people ("team passwords") are not allowed because you cannot tell who used the account, and shared credentials are more likely to be compromised.
Why does this exist: If everyone logs in using the same password and if a critical change is made, there is no way to identify who did it.
Conditions: In order to maintain accurate audit logs transactional services or services that allows users to update, delete and mantain records should all follow this rule
What needs to happen: People must not share passwords. Everyone should use their own account so actions can be traced to a specific individual and the risk of credential theft is reduced.

Action: All administrative and privileged access (Cloud Consoles, Prod DBs, CI/CD Admin) MUST be protected by MFA to prevent account takeover and mass compromise.
What it means: Anyone with powerful access to systems, infrastructure, databases, cloud platforms, or deployment pipelines must use Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), not just a username and password.
Why does this exist: Because compromising one privileged account can affect entire services.
Conditions: This applies specifically to administrative and privileged accounts. It is triggered when a user has elevated permissions
What needs to happen: If an account can administer systems, access sensitive production resources, or make significant changes, MFA must be enforced.
Any other notes: Powerful access means accounts that can make significant changes, portal admins etc, they have much more power than normal user accounts. Cloud consoles are used to create and delete resources. Prod DBs are production databases SQL server, Azure SQL, PostgreSql etc. CI/CD admin is a pipeline administrator, these systems control what gets deployed to production. MFA is multifactor authentication. One privileged account can affect entire services

Action: "Break-glass" accounts MUST be disabled by default and alert immediately upon usage to prevent abuse and unauthorised use.
What it means: Emergency ("break-glass") accounts should not be available for everyday use. They should only be enabled or used in exceptional situations, and any use of them should generate an immediate alert so it can be investigated.
Why does this exist:
Because break-glass accounts are:
- Necessary for recovery during emergencies.
- Extremely powerful, making them attractive targets for attackers.
Conditions: Applies to Identity platforms, Cloud Platform administration, Privileged access management systems, CI/CD  and source control platforms and production infrastructure
What needs to happen: Emergency administrator accounts should only be used as a last resort. They should not be active for normal work, and whenever they are used, the security team should be alerted immediately so any misuse can be detected and investigated.
Any other notes: Break glass account is a highly privileged emergency account that can be used when normal access methods fail. Admins locked out of Microsoft entra, MFA unavailable etc

Action: Standing admin rights MUST NOT exist; Just-in-Time (JIT) or Least Privilege scoping MUST be used to limit the potential damage an attacker can inflict.
What it means: People should not permanently have administrator access. Instead, admin permissions should only be granted when needed (Just-in-Time) or restricted to the minimum permissions required (Least Privilege)
Why does this exist: To limit the potential damage an attacker can inflict
Conditions: Wherever privileged access exists
What needs to happen: People should not walk around with permanent administrator privileges. Give the minimum permissions needed, and where elevated access is required, grant it temporarily and remove it automatically when the task is complete.
Any other notes: Just in Time (JIT) means admin access is granted only when required. Least privilege, give people only the permissions they actually need.

Action: Legacy, non-MFA compatible authentication protocols (e.g., POP3, IMAP, SMTP) MUST be explicitly disabled because they eliminate easy ways for hackers to bypass strong MFA.
What it means: Older authentication methods that do not support Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) must be turned off so attackers cannot use them to avoid MFA protections.
Why does this exist:
- Passwords are frequently stolen through phishing attacks.
- MFA is one of the most effective defences against account compromise.
- Legacy protocols can undermine MFA.
- Attackers specifically target old authentication methods because they are easier to exploit.
Conditions: Any service that uses older authentication methods and do not support MFA
What needs to happen: Turn off old sign-in methods that only use usernames and passwords, because they can allow attackers to access accounts without going through MFA. The organisation should actively block these protocols rather than simply hoping nobody uses them.
Any other notes:
These are older email and access protocols such as:
- POP3 (Post Office Protocol)
- IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol)
- SMTP Authentication (used to send email)
- Older Exchange protocols
- Basic Authentication methods using only a username and password

Action: Service-to-service communication MUST use managed identities or short-lived tokens (Machine Identity); hardcoded keys MUST NOT be used to prevent permanent key theft.
What it means: When one system talks to another system, it should authenticate using managed identities or temporary credentials. It should not use long-lived passwords, secrets, or API keys stored in code or configuration files.
Why does this exist: To prevent permanent key theft which means an attacker could have access for months when there arent stored credentials its much harder for an attacker
Conditions: When one application talks to another, applications accessing Azure, service accesses a database, APIs authenticate to other APIs and when CI/CD pipelines deploy infrastructure
What needs to happen: Whenever systems authenticate to other systems, use managed identities or temporary tokens instead of passwords, API keys, or connection strings embedded in code

Action: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) MUST be mandatory for ALL externally accessible users without exception because it is the single best way to stop account takeover.
What it means: Anyone who can access a service from outside the organisation's network must use Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA). A password alone is not sufficient.
Why does this exist:
Most account compromises start with:
- Phishing
- Password reuse
- Credential stuffing
- Stolen passwords
- Malware
Conditions: Applies to users accessing services from outside the organisation's internal network
What needs to happen: If a user can sign in to a system from outside the organisation, MFA must be enabled for that account.

Action: Shared Accounts MUST NOT be used; every action MUST be traceable to a specific named user or Service Principal to ensure accountability for all system changes.
What it means: Every user, administrator, application, or automated process must have its own identity. You should never use generic shared accounts because it must always be possible to identify who performed an action.
Why does this exist: For accountability and security investigations. With individual accounts the audit trail is clear and seeing when, who and where people make changes supports security investigations
Conditions: Wherever authentication exists
What needs to happen: Don't use generic usernames that multiple people share. Every human should have their own account, and every application should have its own service identity

Action: Single Sign-On (SSO) MUST be used  where possible to reduce password fatigue and simplify the adoption of MFA.
What it means: Users should sign in once with their organisational account (for example, their DfE Entra ID/Microsoft 365 account) and then be able to access approved systems without managing separate usernames and passwords for each application.
Why does this exist: Better security. instead of 20 apps and 20 passwords we have 1 identity and 1 MFA process. Better governance means one someone leaves the ID is disabled and access is removed everywhere
Conditions: Wherever authentication exists
What needs to happen: Wherever possible, applications should use the organisation's central identity provider (such as Microsoft Entra ID) rather than separate usernames and passwords
Any other notes:
- What are the exceptions here? A legacy application doesn't support SSO.
- A supplier doesn't offer SSO integration.
- The cost of enabling SSO is disproportionate
Why is this an obligation if there are exceptions?

Action: All Identity logs (Sign-ins, Failures), Cloud Audit Trails (config changes), and Application Error logs MUST go to the Central SIEM to ensure comprehensive breach detection and investigation.
What it means: Important security, audit, and application logs must be collected in SIEM the central monitoring platform so the security team can detect attacks, investigate incidents, and understand what happened.
Why does this exist:
- Security incidents can be detected quickly.
- Investigators have evidence when something goes wrong.
- Suspicious activity can be correlated across multiple systems.
- Regulatory and audit requirements can be met.
- Attackers cannot hide their actions by exploiting gaps between different logging systems
Conditions: All services that use authentication, cloud storage and applications
What needs to happen: All sign-in logs, cloud configuration change logs, and application logs must be sent to SIEM

Action: Services MUST have an out-of-hours on-call contact for critical service incident escalation to ensure immediate action can be taken during high-risk periods.
What it means: Every service must have someone available to be contacted outside normal working hours in case a serious incident occurs and urgent action is needed.
Why does this exist:
- Critical incidents can happen at any time.
- Fast response often reduces damage and recovery time.
- Security teams need someone who understands the service.
- Business-critical services may require 24/7 support arrangements.
What needs to happen: Every service must have a person or team that can be contacted outside normal working hours so that serious incidents can be responded to immediately rather than waiting until the next working day.
Any other notes: What kinds of service does this link to ciriticality or transactional services?

Action: Log Retention MUST be 90 Days Hot / 1 Year Cold (managed centrally) to ensure sufficient evidence is available for all security incident investigations.
What it means: Security and audit logs must be kept in a searchable format for at least 90 days and archived for at least 1 year, so investigators have enough evidence if a security incident is discovered.
Why does this exist: For incident investigations security teams need to know when the attack started, which accounts were affected, what data was accessed etc. Many organisations need to be able to demonstrate security monitoring and the logs support this
Conditions: Services that use cloud storage solutions, there may be some other conditions
What needs to happen: Keep logs readily searchable for at least 90 days and retain them in archive form for at least 1 year.
Any other notes: Hot storage means logs can be searched immediately, and quick to retrieve. Cold storage means logs are archived, slower to access and usually lower cost

Action: Physical or logical separation of admin privileges is REQUIRED to prevent a simple phishing email from compromising everything.
What it means: The account you use for everyday activities (email, Teams, web browsing) should be separate from the account you use to administer systems.
Why does this exist: Most major incidents start with a compromised user account, separating the privileged admin account means the breach is contain and isnt service wide
Conditions:
Any service that has privileged admin access, or elevated permissions
- Azure Administrators
- Entra ID Administrators
- Microsoft 365 Administrators
- Database Administrators
- GitHub Administrators
- Azure DevOps Administrators
- Server Administrators
- Security Tool Administrators
What needs to happen: Administrators should use separate accounts (and sometimes separate devices) for privileged activities.

Action: Administrative work is ONLY permitted on Managed, Encrypted, EDR-protected devices to ensure the highest level of security for high-privilege operations.
What it means: If you're performing administrative tasks, you must do so from a company-approved device that is managed, encrypted, and actively monitored by security tooling. You must not administer systems from personal, unmanaged, or insecure devices.
Why does this exist: We do not want high-privilege accounts being used from personal or unmanaged devices because compromising the device could lead directly to a major security breach.
Conditions: Any activity performed using a privileged account
What needs to happen: If you're carrying out administrative or privileged activities, you must use a secure corporate-managed device that is encrypted and monitored by EDR.

Action: Any suspected breach, lost device, or accidental data exposure MUST be reported to CISD immediately to ensure a small incident does not become a major breach
What it means: If you think a security incident might have happened, don't try to decide how serious it is yourself. Report it to CISD immediately so it can be investigated and managed before it gets worse.
Why does this exist: Early reporting gives the organisation the best chance of containing the issue before it turns into a major security incident or data breach.
Conditions: Any service that has a data breach
What needs to happen: If something security-related happens, or you think it might have happened, tell CISD immediately.

Action: All staff MUST complete Security Awareness training annually because staff are the best defence against human error.
What it means: Every employee must complete security awareness training at least once a year so they understand common cyber risks and know how to avoid causing or contributing to security incidents.
Why does this exist: Many security incidents involve human actions rather than technical failures.
Conditions: All staff are required to complete the training
What needs to happen: Everyone must complete cyber security awareness training every year so they can recognise threats, handle information safely, and help prevent incidents caused by mistakes or social engineering attacks.

Action: All services MUST have local incident response plans aligned to the CISD standard to ensure consistency in handling and escalating incidents.
What it means: Every service must have its own documented plan for responding to security incidents, and that plan must follow the standards and processes defined by CISD so that incidents are handled consistently across the organisation.
Why does this exist: During an incident people are under pressure and may not know who to call, what actions to take, who can approve decisions or when to involve CISD, A documented plan avoids confusion
What needs to happen: Every service needs a documented playbook for responding to incidents, and it must follow the organisation's CISD incident management approach so that security incidents are handled quickly, consistently, and with the right escalation route
Any other notes: Are there specific services that need this or is it all services?

Action: All stateful data MUST be backed up to a separate region/location (Immutable backups preferred) to ensure all systems and data can be recovered after a major attack or disaster.
What it means: Any data that changes and needs to be retained must be backed up, and those backups must be stored somewhere separate from the primary system. Ideally, the backups should be immutable (cannot be changed or deleted) so they can still be recovered after a ransomware attack or major outage.
Why does this exist: The goal is to ensure the service can recover from ransomware, accidental deletion, corruption, or a major disaster.
Conditions: Definitely services that use cloud storage, I am not sure if we have any on-prem legacy services and what the rules would be for that
What needs to happen: Any important data must be backed up and stored separately from production systems. Ideally, the backups should be immutable so attackers cannot delete them.

Action: Business important and critical services MUST span Availbility Zones (AZs) to ensure resilience against major cloud failures
Restoration capability MUST be tested/proved annually (Drills) because a backup that is never tested is not a backup.
What it means: It's not enough to create backups. The organisation must regularly prove that those backups can actually be restored successfully.
Why does this exist: Because many organisations discover problems only when they need the backup.
Conditions: Any service that backs up their data
What needs to happen: Don't just create backups and assume they're fine. At least once a year, prove that you can successfully restore systems and data so that, during a real incident, recovery is reliable and predictable.

Action: Incident response plans SHOULD be tested on an annual basis to ensure people are familiar with the process under pressure.
What it means: Service teams should practise responding to security incidents at least once a year so that, if a real incident occurs, people know what to do and can respond quickly and effectively
Why does this exist: People discover during a real incident that contact lists are out of date, nobody knows who owns the service, escalation paths are unclear and people have never read the plan,. Testing helps identify those issues before a real emergency
Conditions: Every service
What needs to happen: Don't wait for a real cyber incident to discover whether your response process works. Practise it at least annually so that the people involved know their roles and can respond confidently when under pressure.

Action: Base container images MUST be pulled from a trusted internal registry and MUST be refreshed/patched at least monthly to prevent systems from being built using old, vulnerable software components.
What it means: When building containerised applications (e.g., Docker containers), teams must use approved base images from the organisation's trusted registry, and those images must be updated regularly so new deployments aren't built on top of vulnerable software.
Why does this exist: To prevent systems from being built using old, vulnerable software components
Conditions: Services using containers, kubernetes, Docker, AKS, container apps and other containerised workloads. Not applicable to SaaS products you dont build, standard sharepoint solutions conventional virtual machines that dont use containers
What needs to happen: If you're deploying containers, use approved base images from the organisation's trusted registry and update those images regularly.
Any other notes: Containers are like a shipping container, it runs on the idea build it once and run it anywhere. You build everything within that container and then whatever is inside that container travels together. So you can lift and shift your application within that container to any environment. A base container image is the foundational image that provides the operating system and runtime environment for your containerised application, and everything built on top inherits its configuration, dependencies, and security posture.

Action: Operating Systems and runtimes MUST be patched regularly, with Critical patches = 14 Days and High = 30 Days SLA, to ensure known flaws are fixed before hackers can exploit them.
What it means: Servers, operating systems, and software runtimes must be kept up to date, and serious security vulnerabilities must be fixed within defined timeframes before attackers can exploit them.
Why does this exist: To ensure known flaws are fixed before hackers can exploit them
Conditions: Servers, virtual machines, operating systems, container hosts, application runtimes and cloud compute instances. Usually less applicable to fully managed SaaS products where the supplier patches the underlying operating systems and runtime
What needs to happen: Keep operating systems and software platforms up to date. Critical security vulnerabilities must be fixed within 14 days and High vulnerabilities within 30 days so attackers can't exploit known weaknesses that already have a fix available.

Action: The use of End-of-Life software is PROHIBITED because it contains unpatchable flaws that are easy for hackers to compromise.
What it means: You must not use software that is no longer supported by the vendor, because security vulnerabilities will no longer be fixed and attackers actively target these systems.
Why does this exist: Security teams generally consider EOL software to be a significant risk because it creates a situation where, even if you know about a vulnerability, you cannot properly remediate it
Conditions: Any service that uses end of life software, which means the vendor has stopped supporting the product, e.g unsupported versions of windows server, outdated Java runtime, an old version of SQL server
What needs to happen: Upgrade the software and ensure there is funding available
Any other notes: End of life means no security patches, no bug fixes, no technical support and no feature updates. When software becomes EOL the vendor will usually offer discounts or incentives to procure the new version of the EOL software you have or provide information on similar software offered by other vendors

Action: Have you consulted relevant security stakeholders when developing your business case?
What it means: Have you spoken to the people who are responsible for security and technology to get their input while creating the business case?
Why does this exist: Project teams often do not have specialist security expertise. Security stakeholders can identify risks, obligations, costs, and requirements that might otherwise be missed. The guidance specifically states that the SRO, service owner, business analyst, CTO, CISO and technical security assurance teams should contribute to the business case
Conditions:
This applies whenever:
- A new service, product, system or change is being proposed.
- A business case is being developed.
- Security risks or obligations could arise.
What needs to happen:
Evidence should show that relevant security stakeholders were engaged, for example:
- Discussions with Security, Cyber, Architecture or Assurance teams.
- Review meetings.
- Feedback incorporated into the business case.
- Approval or endorsement from appropriate security representatives.
Guidance:
https://www.security.gov.uk/policy-and-guidance/secure-by-design/activities/considering-security-within-the-business-case/

Service Engagement Form

Procurements and suppliers – security considerations

Action: Does the business case include cyber security considerations?
What it means: Does the business case clearly explain any security requirements, risks, controls, obligations and costs associated with the proposal?
Why does this exist: Security affects scope, delivery time, resources, funding and user trust. If these considerations are not identified early, projects can be delayed, become more expensive, or introduce unacceptable risks. The guidance states that security should be included throughout the business case so that the true costs and effort are understood from the outset
Conditions:
All business cases involving:
- Digital services.
- Technology solutions.
- Data processing.
- Third-party technology suppliers.
What needs to happen:
The business case should include security information such as:
- Security obligations (legal, regulatory, policy).
- Threats and risks.
- Security controls.
- Resource requirements.
- Security governance arrangements.
- Security-related costs

Action: Does the economic case include an analysis with the security threats, security risk tolerance, security objectives and cyber resilience as part of critical success factors?
What it means:
When comparing options, have you assessed:
- What security threats exist?
- How much risk the organisation is willing to accept?
- What security outcomes need to be achieved?
- How resilient the service needs to be?
- Whether these factors influence which option is the best choice?
Why does this exist: A cheaper option is not necessarily the best option if it exposes the organisation to significant cyber risk. The economic case should consider security impacts when deciding which option delivers the greatest overall value. The guidance states that the economic case should include information about security threats and assess resilience against security attacks as part of the success criteria.
Conditions:
This is relevant when:
- Comparing multiple delivery options.
- Assessing value for money.
- Producing economic appraisals under Green Book principles.
What needs to happen:
The economic case should show:
- Key cyber threats.
- Defined risk appetite or risk tolerance.
- Security objectives.
- Resilience requirements.
- How security contributes to critical success factors.
- How these considerations were used to evaluate options.

Action: Does the economic case consider varying levels of security when calculating value for money?
What it means: Have you considered how different levels of security investment affect costs, risks and benefits?
Why does this exist:
Security is not all-or-nothing. Different options may provide:
- Basic security.
- Enhanced security.
- High-assurance security.
Each level has different costs and benefits. The guidance states that making security integral to scope, delivery and implementation should be assessed as part of achieving value for money.
Conditions:
When:
- Assessing options.
- Developing cost-benefit analyses.
- Determining preferred solutions.
What needs to happen:
You should demonstrate:
- Security was included in option appraisals.
- Different security levels were assessed where appropriate.
- Costs of security controls were considered.
- Costs of security incidents or failures were considered.
- The selected option provides an appropriate balance between cost and security

Action: Does the management case include details of the security governance and assurance approach?
What it means: Have you explained who will oversee security, how security decisions will be made, and how you will check security is working throughout delivery?
Why does this exist: Security cannot simply be designed and forgotten. There must be ongoing governance, monitoring and assurance to ensure controls continue to work and risks remain managed. The guidance states that the management case should define security roles and responsibilities, governance arrangements, risk management processes, change assessment processes and security assurance activities
Conditions:
Applies during:
- Project delivery.
- Transition to live service.
- Live operation.
- Change management activities.
What needs to happen:
The management case should include:
- Security governance structure.
- Security roles and responsibilities.
- Risk management processes.
- Security assurance activities and reviews.
- Change control processes.
- Testing and validation arrangements.
- Monitoring and reporting mechanisms.

Action: Does the project have a resource plan showing security roles and skills required to support the delivery of the service?
What it means: Have you documented who is needed to support security on the project, what they will do, and what skills they need?
Why does this exist: Security activities do not happen automatically. Projects need suitably skilled people available at the right time. Without planning for security resources, key activities such as threat modelling, security architecture reviews, security testing and risk management may not happen. The guidance requires a comprehensive security resource plan covering the people involved throughout the project lifecycle.
Conditions:
Applies when:
- Creating a new service.
- Delivering significant changes.
- Preparing business cases and project plans.
- Seeking funding or approvals.
What needs to happen:
There should be a documented security resource plan showing:
- Security roles required.
- Key responsibilities.
- Required skills and expertise.
- When resources are needed.
- Whether resources are internal, shared or externally contracted.
- Estimated effort and costs

Action: Have you identified and captured the skills required to carry out security activities and engaged with your organisation's security team to support the delivery?
What it means: Do you know what security expertise is needed, and have you involved the people in your organisation who can provide it?
Why does this exist: Many project teams do not contain all the specialist skills required for Secure by Design. The guidance specifically recommends consulting security professionals, security architects, CTOs, CISOs and other specialists to identify required skills and provide support
Conditions:
Applies when:
- Security-related activities are planned.
- Specialist security knowledge is required.
- Internal capability gaps may exist.
What needs to happen:
You should be able to show:
- A list of required security skills.
- Which activities need those skills.
- Evidence of engagement with security teams.
- Plans for training if skills are missing.
- Assigned individuals or teams for key security activities

Action: Have you identified and captured the required technology resources such as software development environments, tools and security capabilities that will be required for the project?
What it means: Have you worked out what security tools, platforms and technical capabilities will be needed to build and operate the service securely?
Why does this exist: Security depends on more than people. Projects often require specialist tools and infrastructure to support secure development, testing, monitoring and operations. The guidance requires teams to assess and document the technology resources needed.
Conditions:
Applies when:
- Planning delivery.
- Designing technical solutions.
- Estimating project costs.
- Operating live services.
What needs to happen:
The project should identify:
- Existing organisational security capabilities.
- Additional tools required.
- Development and testing environments.
- Monitoring and detection capabilities.
- Identity and access management tooling.
- Security testing tools

Action: Have you considered pre-approved or recommended architectural patterns available from your organisation or other government departments?
What it means: Before designing something new, did you check whether there is already a recognised secure design pattern that could be reused?
Why does this exist: DfE does have approved architectures, security patterns and reference designs that have already been reviewed and assessed. Reusing these approaches reduces risk, improves consistency and avoids unnecessary design effort. The guidance encourages using existing organisational capabilities, policies, procedures and resources where possible
Conditions:
Applies when:
- Designing a new solution.
- Selecting technology.
- Creating target architecture.
- Implementing security controls.
What needs to happen:
You should be able to demonstrate that you have:
- Reviewed relevant organisational standards.
- Considered existing government patterns and frameworks.
- Assessed whether approved architectures meet project needs.
- Documented any decision to deviate from established patterns.

Action: Have you assigned the Secure by Design responsibilities (for example, in a RACI matrix) and communicated them to the relevant parties?
What it means:
Have you clearly defined who is responsible for each security activity, and made sure everyone understands their role?
In other words:
- Who does the work?
- Who approves the work?
- Who needs to be consulted?
- Who needs to be kept informed?
The guidance recommends using a RACI matrix to make this clear. A RACI identifies who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for each activity
Why does this exist:
Security activities often fail because everyone assumes someone else is dealing with them.
The guidance states that agreeing responsibilities helps organisations:
- assign ownership of security activities
- identify skills and resource gaps
- make individuals personally responsible for managing cyber risk
Conditions:
This applies:
- At the start of a project.
- When delivery teams are formed.
- When responsibilities change.
- When new security activities are introduced.
- During periodic project reviews.
What needs to happen: Responsibilities have been identified,

Action: Have you appointed a Senior Responsible Owner (SRO), service owner or equivalent, and informed the individual of their responsibilities?
What it means:
Has someone been formally made accountable for the security risks and security outcomes of the service?
This person doesn't necessarily perform security activities themselves, but they are ultimately accountable for ensuring they happen.
The guidance identifies the Senior Responsible Owner (SRO) and Service Owner as key roles for agreeing and overseeing security responsibilities.
Why does this exist:
Without a clearly accountable person:
- Security decisions may be delayed.
- Risks may remain unresolved.
- Nobody owns difficult decisions.
- Security issues can fall between teams.
Secure by Design promotes clear accountability for cyber risk from the beginning of delivery.
Conditions:
Applies whenever:
- A service is being developed.
- A major change is being delivered.
- A programme or project requires governance.
- Cyber risks need ownership.
What needs to happen: An accountable individual must be identified, and responsibilities must be clearly explained.

Action: Have you included continuous assurance processes in the service's project delivery workflow?
What it means: Have you built regular security checks and reviews into the way the project is delivered, rather than only checking security at the end?
Why does this exist: Traditional projects often perform a single security review shortly before go-live. Secure by Design requires security to be continually assessed throughout the service lifecycle because threats, risks and designs change over time. Continuous assurance helps identify issues early and provides confidence that security remains effective.
Conditions:
This applies whenever:
- A service is being designed, built or maintained.
- Agile delivery methods are used.
- Technology or business requirements are changing.
- Security controls need ongoing validation.
What needs to happen:
Evidence might include:
- Security reviews built into sprint cycles.
- Security checkpoints within delivery governance.
- Threat assessments being regularly reviewed.
- Security testing occurring throughout development.
- Regular risk reviews.
- Assurance activities included in project plans.

Action: Have you used the organisation's risk appetite statements and applied them to the nature of the service to determine the security risk appetite level for the project?
What it means: Have you taken your organisation's existing risk appetite and worked out what it means for this specific service or project?
Why does this exist:
Different organisations tolerate different levels of risk.
For example:
- A public information website may tolerate more risk.
- A system holding sensitive personal data may tolerate very little risk.
- A payment service may have almost no tolerance for integrity failures.
Without a defined risk appetite:
- Teams make inconsistent decisions.
- Security investments become difficult to justify.
- Risks may be accepted unintentionally.
The guidance states that a project risk appetite helps determine acceptable and unacceptable risks and supports informed risk management decisions
Conditions:
This applies when:
- A service is being planned.
- Discovery is underway.
- Security requirements are being established.
- Risk assessments are being performed.
The guidance says this should be established during Discovery (or requirements gathering) and reviewed whenever major changes occur.
What needs to happen: You should be able to show DfEs risk appetite was reviewed, the service specific implications were identified, a project level risk appetite statement was produced, and the statement was approved and shared

Action: Have you established a clear governance structure around risk management decision making?
What it means: Is it clear who makes risk decisions, who approves risk acceptance, who escalates risks and who monitors them?
Why does this exist:
Good risk management requires accountability.
Without governance:
- Risks may be ignored.
- Risks may be accepted by someone without authority.
- Important decisions may be delayed.
- Different teams may use different standards.
The guidance emphasises that the risk appetite must be communicated and used by delivery teams to support risk management decision-making and governance
Conditions: Applies whenever Security risks are are being assessed, being escalated, and accepted. Also when Security decisions affect project delivery
What needs to happen: The governance model should explain, who owns risks, who approves risk acceptance, and how escalation works

Action: Have you considered the risk appetite of any organisations the service shares or exchanges data with?
What it means: If your service shares data with another organisation, have you considered whether they have stricter security requirements or lower tolerance for risk than you do?
Why does this exist:
A service may interact with:
- Other government departments
- Local authorities
- Arm's length bodies
- Suppliers
- Partner organisations
A risk that seems acceptable internally may be unacceptable to a partner organisation.
The guidance highlights the need to understand dependencies and how other projects or organisations influence risk management decisions.
Conditions:
Applies when:
- Data is shared externally.
- Systems are integrated.
- Services rely on third parties.
- Multiple organisations are involved.
What needs to happen: Consider data sharing arrangements, partner organisations expectations, and differences in risk appetite

Action: Have you considered whether the service is part of the Critical National Infrastructure (CNI) or fundamental to the organisation's output and missions?
What it means: Have you assessed how important the service is to government operations or national infrastructure?.. What happens if this service fails or is compromised?
Why does this exist: Not all services have the same consequences if they fail, some may have a low impact some may have high impact.
Conditions:
Relevant whenever a service:
- Supports critical operations.
- Processes critical data.
- Provides essential services.
- Supports departmental missions.
- Could cause significant operational disruption if unavailable.
What needs to happen: You should assess Service Criticality, national impact and required resilience

Action: Have you considered the appropriate Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) profile for all the components of the service?
What it means: Have you worked out what level of assurance and security expectations apply to each part of the service based on its risk and importance?
Why does this exist: Different components may require different levels of security.
Conditions:
Applies when:
- Designing the service architecture.
- Selecting controls.
- Planning assurance activities.
- Determining security requirements.
What needs to happen: Assess each major service component, appropriate CAF expectations, traceability, provide evidence in CAF assessment, security architecture documents etc

Action: Have you reviewed the security risks of any cloud technology (such as IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) before using it?
What it means:
Before deciding to use a cloud service, have you assessed the security risks it might introduce?
- Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
- Platform as a Service (PaaS)
- Software as a Service (SaaS)
Why does this exist:
Cloud services can introduce risks relating to:
- Data protection
- Access control
- Supplier security
- Resilience and availability
- Data location
- Regulatory compliance
Secure by Design requires organisations to perform security due diligence on third-party technology products before relying on them.
Conditions:
Applies whenever the service uses IaaS, PaaS and SaaS:
- Microsoft Azure
- AWS
- Google Cloud
- SaaS products
- Cloud-hosted platforms
- Cloud storage services
What needs to happen:
You should assess:
- What information will be stored?
- Who can access the environment?
- Where is the data hosted?
- What security certifications exist?
- What security controls are provided?
- What risks remain?

Action: Have you identified the security risks related to third-party Managed Service Providers (MSPs) prior to using them?
What it means: Before appointing an external provider to deliver or operate services on your behalf, have you assessed the risks they introduce?
Why does this exist:
MSPs often receive significant access to:
- Systems
- Infrastructure
- Data
- Administrative accounts
A security weakness within the MSP can become a security weakness in your service.
Secure by Design requires security due diligence on third-party providers
Conditions:
Applies when:
- Outsourcing support services
- Using managed hosting
- Using managed security services
- Using outsourced operational teams
What needs to happen:
You should assess:
- Supplier security maturity
- Access management controls
- Incident response capabilities
- Personnel vetting
- Monitoring arrangements
- Business continuity arrangements

Action: Have you assessed and managed the risks associated with any third-party development environments or software prior to committing to using them?
What it means: Before using external development tools, frameworks, code repositories or software products, have you checked whether they introduce security risks?
Why does this exist:
Development tools can create risks such as:
- Software supply-chain attacks
- Vulnerable dependencies
- Malicious code
- Insecure build pipelines
- Exposure of source code
Conditions:
Applies when using:
- GitHub
- GitLab
- CI/CD platforms
- Development frameworks
- Open-source libraries
- Code generation tools
What needs to happen:
You should assess:
- Supplier reputation
- Known vulnerabilities
- Security updates process
- Dependency risks
- Access controls
- Licence implications

Action: Have you created a report that highlights any security risks associated with using third-party products, including recommendations on how to manage those risks?
What it means: Have you formally documented the risks introduced by third-party products and explained how those risks will be managed?
Why does this exist:
Decision makers need visibility of supplier risks before approving technology choices.
The report provides evidence that due diligence has been completed and allows risk owners to make informed decisions
Conditions:
Applies whenever:
- Third-party products are used.
- Security risks are identified.
- Procurement decisions are being made.
What needs to happen:
The report should contain:
- Product description
- Identified risks
- Impact assessment
- Risk ratings
- Proposed mitigations
- Residual risks
- Recommendations

Action: Have you discussed security obligations, including government policies, regulations, laws and contracts, for your service with your organisation's compliance or information security teams?
What it means:
Have you spoken to the people who understand legal, regulatory and security requirements to determine what rules your service must follow?
The guidance specifically recommends consulting legal, commercial and information management teams alongside security specialists
Why does this exist:
Different services have different obligations.
For example:
- UK GDPR
- Data Protection Act
- PCI-DSS
- Government Security Policies
- Supplier contracts
Missing a requirement can lead to non-compliance, fines or operational risk
What needs to happen:
Evidence could include:
- Compliance workshops
- Legal reviews
- Security reviews
- Governance meeting outputs

Action: Have you fed compliance requirements into risk management activities?
What it means: Have you used compliance requirements to influence your risk assessments, controls and mitigation plans?
Why does this exist: Compliance requirements often represent risks. Secure by Design expects obligations to be incorporated into service design and risk management.
What needs to happen:
You should be able to trace:
Requirement → Risk → Control

Action: Have you met obligations in relation to personally identifiable information (PII) being processed, stored or transmitted by the service?
What it means: If the system uses personal information, have you met all legal and security requirements for protecting it?
Why does this exist: Personal information requires special protection under privacy and data protection laws
Conditions:
Any services that use PII: Examples:
- Names
- Addresses
- National Insurance numbers
- Contact details
- Employee records
What needs to happen:
Typically:
- Data minimisation applied
- Appropriate security controls implemented
- Retention arrangements defined
- DPIA completed where required

Action: Have you met obligations in relation to financial information (such as credit card details) being processed, stored or transmitted by the service?
What it means: If the service handles financial data, have you complied with the relevant security and regulatory requirements?
Why does this exist: Financial data is often highly attractive to attackers and subject to additional controls.
Conditions:
Any services that use financial data:
- Credit card details
- Bank account information
- Payment records
- Financial transactions
What needs to happen:
Examples:
- PCI-DSS compliance where applicable
- Encryption
- Strong access control
- Secure transmission

Action: Have you met obligations in relation to intellectual property (IP) data being processed, stored or transmitted by the service?
What it means: If the system handles intellectual property, have you implemented the protections required to safeguard it?
Why does this exist:
Loss of intellectual property can:
- Harm the organisation
- Create legal liabilities
- Damage commercial value
What needs to happen:
You should understand:
- Ownership arrangements
- Licensing restrictions
- Contractual obligations
- Security classification requirements

Action: Have you documented the legal, regulatory and contractual requirements that must be met by the service?
What it means: Have you created a list of all the rules, laws, regulations and contractual commitments that the service must comply with?
Why does this exist:
Teams cannot comply with requirements they have not identified.
The obligations profile should be documented and shared across the project.
What needs to happen:
You should maintain a record showing:
- Applicable laws
- Regulations
- Government policies
- Standards
- Contract obligations

Action: Have you ensured that other organisations you plan to share data with as part of the service delivery are compliant with the relevant cyber security obligations?
What it means: Before sharing information with another organisation, have you checked they meet the required security standards?
Why does this exist:
Your security obligations do not disappear when data leaves your organisation.
The receiving organisation must also be capable of protecting the information appropriately.
Conditions: Any service that shares data with another organisation
What needs to happen:
You should assess:
- Security controls
- Compliance status
- Relevant certifications
- Data handling arrangements

Action: Have you defined data sharing agreements with any organisations you are sharing data with?
What it means: Have you formally agreed how shared data will be protected, used and managed?
Why does this exist: Data sharing creates accountability and legal obligations that need to be documented.
What needs to happen:
A data sharing agreement should normally define:
- Purpose of sharing
- Types of data
- Security controls
- Retention arrangements
- Incident reporting
- Responsibilities

Action: If data will be processed, stored or transmitted outside the UK or the European Economic Area (EEA), have you considered the relevant security obligations?
What it means: If information leaves the UK or EEA, have you checked what legal and security requirements apply?
Why does this exist:
Cross-border data movement may create additional legal and privacy obligations.
Secure by Design requires teams to understand applicable obligations based on the nature of the service and its data.
What needs to happen:
You should assess:
- Where data is stored
- International transfer mechanisms
- Legal restrictions
- Supplier arrangements

Action: Have you completed a Data Protection and Impact Assessment (DPIA)?
