What it means: Have you formally assessed how the service affects people's privacy and identified actions needed to protect personal data?
Why does this exist: A DPIA helps identify privacy risks before a service is implemented and ensures appropriate safeguards are designed into the service from the outset.
Conditions:
Usually required when:
- Processing personal data
- Introducing new technology
- Conducting large-scale processing
- Monitoring individuals
What needs to happen:
A DPIA should:
- Describe the processing
- Identify privacy risks
- Assess impacts on individuals
- Define mitigations
- Be reviewed by appropriate specialists

Action: Have you taken business objectives into account when making security decisions?
What it means: When choosing security controls, have you considered what the service is trying to achieve for the organisation?
Why does this exist:
Security should help the organisation achieve its objectives safely, not get in the way.
If security decisions are made without understanding the business purpose, you can end up with:
- Unnecessary controls
- Increased costs
- Delays to delivery
- Reduced business benefits
Conditions:
This applies when:
- Defining security requirements
- Designing security controls
- Making architecture decisions
- Prioritising risks
- Designing operational processes
What needs to happen:
You should be able to show that:
- Business objectives were identified.
- Security requirements were linked to those objectives.
- Security decisions considered business impact.
- Any trade-offs between security and business needs were documented.

Action: Have you taken user needs into account when making security decisions?
What it means: Have you considered how real users will interact with security controls and whether those controls are practical and usable?
Why does this exist:
Poorly designed security controls often lead users to:
- Work around the controls
- Circumvent processes
- Make mistakes
- Become frustrated
Conditions:
This applies when designing:
- Authentication processes
- Access controls
- User journeys
- Security policies
- Business processes
What needs to happen:
You should be able to demonstrate that:
- User research was considered.
- Security requirements were balanced against usability.
- User groups were identified.
- Controls were designed around how users actually work.
- User needs continue to be reviewed as the service evolves.

Action: Have you identified and documented the business and technology information assets in scope of the service?
What it means: Have you made a list of everything valuable that the service uses, stores, manages or depends on?
Why does this exist:
You cannot protect assets if you do not know they exist.
The guidance states that documenting assets helps organisations:
- Understand what needs protecting.
- Manage risks and vulnerabilities.
- Identify accountability.
- Assess the impact of loss or compromise.
Conditions:
This applies from:
- Discovery
- Requirements gathering
- Design
- Build
- Live operation
Asset information should also be reviewed whenever the service changes.
What needs to happen:
Create and maintain an inventory of assets in scope such as:
Business assets
- Customer data
- Employee information
- Financial records
- Intellectual property
Technology assets
- Applications
- Servers
- Databases
- APIs
- Networks
- Cloud environments
It should also be reviewed and maintained as the service evolves

Action: Have you identified and documented a service owner or information asset owner for each asset?
What it means: Does every important asset have a named person responsible for it?
Why does this exist:
If nobody owns an asset:
- Security issues may not be addressed.
- Risks may not be reviewed.
- Decisions may be delayed.
- Vulnerabilities may remain unmanaged.
The guidance specifically highlights the need to understand who is responsible for each asset so that accountability for protection is clear.
Conditions:
Applies to all assets identified within the service, including:
- Data assets
- Applications
- Infrastructure
- Platforms
- Shared services
What needs to happen:
For every asset, there should be:
- A named owner.
- A defined role.
- Accountability for security decisions.
- Responsibility for managing risks relating to the asset.

Action: Have you completed a business impact assessment to determine the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data if the service was compromised?
What it means:
Have you assessed what would happen to the organisation, users and service if its data or systems were:
- Read by unauthorised people (Confidentiality)
- Changed or corrupted (Integrity)
- Unavailable (Availability)
Why does this exist:
Not all information and systems are equally important.
The organisation needs to understand which assets would cause the greatest damage if compromised so it can:
- Prioritise security investment.
- Identify the most important risks.
- Design appropriate security controls.
- Support threat modelling and risk assessments.
Conditions:
This applies when:
- A new service is being developed.
- Existing services are changing significantly.
- Information assets have been identified.
- Security risks are being assessed.
The guidance recommends completing this during discovery or requirements gathering and updating it whenever significant assets change
What needs to happen:
The assessment should consider, confidentiality, integrity and availability. The assessment should document:
- Assets being assessed.
- Impact ratings.
- Consequences of compromise.
- Overall business impact.

Action: Did you consult with business stakeholders when creating the impact assessment?
What it means: Did you involve the people who understand how the service operates and how the organisation would be affected by a security incident?
Why does this exist:
Technical teams understand systems.
Business stakeholders understand:
- Operational impacts.
- Financial impacts.
- Regulatory consequences.
- Reputational damage.
- User impacts.
The guidance specifically recommends involving asset owners, service owners, security professionals and other business stakeholders when assessing asset importance. Workshops and surveys are recommended methods for gathering this information.
Conditions:
Applies whenever:
- An asset evaluation is being completed.
- Business impacts are being scored.
- Security priorities are being established
What needs to happen:
Evidence could include:
- Workshops.
- Interviews.
- Surveys.
- Stakeholder review sessions.
- Sign-off from asset owners or service owners.
The assessment should demonstrate input from relevant stakeholders rather than being produced solely by technical teams

Action: Have you obtained the organisation's overarching threat assessment (or completed your own if there is not one available)?
What it means: Have you identified an existing organisational threat assessment and used it, or created a service-specific threat assessment if none exists?
Why does this exist:
Projects should not start from scratch if the organisation already understands its threat landscape.
The guidance states that many organisations already have threat assessments that can be used as the foundation for service-level assessments. If one is unavailable, a new assessment should be commissioned or produced.
Conditions:
Applies when:
- Starting discovery or alpha phase.
- Performing threat modelling.
- Conducting risk assessments.
- Designing security controls.
The guidance strongly recommends having a threat assessment before threat modelling or risk assessment activities begin.
What needs to happen:
You should:
1. Check whether an organisational threat assessment exists.
2. Obtain and review it.
3. Tailor it to your service if necessary.
4. Create a new assessment if none exists.
5. Keep it updated when the service changes.

Action: Does your threat assessment include the motives, intent and capability of the threat actors relevant to your service?
What it means:
Does your assessment explain:
- Who might attack the service?
- Why they would attack it?
- What they are trying to achieve?
- Whether they have the ability to succeed?
Why does this exist:
Understanding attackers helps teams design proportionate security controls.
Secure by Design states that threat assessments should capture threat actor:
- Motivation
- Intent
- Capability
- Type of threat actor
Conditions:
Applies when:
- Threat assessments are being performed.
- Threat modelling is underway.
- Security controls are being selected.
What needs to happen: The assessment should document threat actors and their motivation, intent, and capability

Action: Have you considered threat intelligence and the history of previous attacks on the organisation (or similar organisations) as part of the threat assessment?
What it means: Have you looked at real-world evidence about attacks that have already happened, either to your organisation or to similar organisations?
Why does this exist:
Threat assessments should be evidence-based rather than based on assumptions.
The guidance states that threat assessments should use:
- Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI)
- Reputable intelligence sources
- Research into previous attacks on the organisation
- Research into attacks against similar organisations
Conditions:
Applies when:
- Producing or updating threat assessments.
- Identifying likely attackers.
- Assessing threat levels.
What needs to happen:
You should demonstrate consideration of:
- Internal security incident history.
- Cyber Threat Intelligence reports.
- NCSC threat reporting.
- Industry intelligence feeds.
- Lessons learned from similar organisations.
- Known attacker tactics and techniques.

Action: Have you documented the technical architecture for the end-to-end service and system?
What it means: Can someone look at your documentation and understand how the whole service works technically, including all the systems, components, integrations and data flows involved?
Why does this exist:
You cannot properly assess security if you do not know what actually makes up the service.
Architecture documentation provides the foundation for the remaining security work. It allows security specialists and delivery teams to determine:
- where sensitive information is stored
- where information enters and leaves the service
- which systems communicate with each other
- where users authenticate
- which components are exposed externally
- where trust boundaries exist
- which third parties are relied upon
- what an attacker could potentially target
Conditions:
This is relevant where a service:
- consists of multiple technical components
- integrates with other systems
- processes or stores information
- uses cloud infrastructure
- exposes APIs or other interfaces
- relies on external suppliers or services
- has different user types or administrative access
- crosses organisational or network boundaries
What needs to happen:
The team should produce and maintain appropriate technical architecture documentation.
That would normally include things such as:
Architecture diagram
Showing the major technical components and how they connect.
Data-flow information
Showing important data moving between components or systems.
Interfaces and integrations
Documenting APIs, third-party systems, identity services and other dependencies.
Trust/security boundaries
Showing where the security context changes, for example between the public internet and an internal environment.
Hosting/infrastructure
Documenting where components are hosted and the major infrastructure involved.
The documentation should also be current. An architecture diagram created early in discovery but no longer representing the live design would not really satisfy the intent of the rule.

Action: Have you identified and documented the possible attack paths or threat events that could be used to exploit vulnerabilities in the service?
What it means: Have you worked out the realistic ways somebody could attack or misuse the service and written them down?
Why does this exist:
Simply identifying technical components is not enough. The team needs to think about, given our architecture what could actually go wrong from a security perspective?
Doing this systematically helps find security weaknesses before they become incidents.
It also helps teams prioritise security investment according to realistic threats rather than simply implementing generic security features.
Conditions:
Threat modelling should consider, where applicable:
- external attackers
- compromised user accounts
- malicious or accidental insider activity
- unauthorised access
- privilege escalation
- vulnerable integrations
- exposed interfaces
- manipulation of information
- disclosure of sensitive information
- service disruption
- compromised dependencies
- misuse of legitimate functionality.
Not every imaginable threat needs to be treated equally. The important point is identifying credible threats relevant to the service and its architecture.
What needs to happen:
The team should carry out a structured threat assessment or threat-modelling exercise.
There should be evidence showing:
1. What is being protected?
    - systems
    - sensitive information
    - user accounts
    - privileged functions
    - critical services.
1. What could threaten it?
    - identified threat events or scenarios.
1. Where could the threat occur?
    - component, interface, data flow or trust boundary.
1. What would happen if it succeeded?
    - impact on confidentiality, integrity or availability.
1. How significant is the threat?
    - some form of evaluation/prioritisation.
The identified threats should be documented and traceable back to the architecture.

Action: Have you identified and documented what security controls are available to reduce the likelihood of threat events?
What it means:
Once you know what could go wrong, this question asks:
Have you worked out what protections can prevent those things from happening, or make them much less likely, and documented them?
Why does this exist:
Identifying threats without deciding what will be done about them does not actually reduce risk.
The intended chain should be:
Threat → Risk → Security control → Reduced risk
It also helps prevent controls being introduced without knowing what problem they are supposed to solve.
Conditions:
For each meaningful threat identified during threat modelling, the team should consider:
- What existing controls already address it?
- Are those controls sufficient?
- Are additional controls required?
- Is the control preventative, detective or corrective?
- Who owns the control?
- Has it actually been implemented?
- How will the team know that it works?
What needs to happen: Ideally, there should be traceability between threats and controls.

Action: Have you identified and documented any security controls that could mitigate multiple threat events?
What it means: Have you looked for security protections that solve more than one of the security problems you identified?
Why does this exist:
This encourages the team to think about security holistically rather than threat-by-threat in isolation.
It can:
- provide stronger defence across the service
- reduce duplicated security solutions
- help prioritise high-value controls
- simplify security architecture
- make security controls easier to maintain
- identify critical controls on which several security protections depend.
Importantly, it can also expose concentration risk.
If ten important threats are all mitigated by one security control, failure
Conditions:
This is particularly relevant once:
1. threats have been identified; and
2. possible security controls have been identified.
The team can then map controls against threats.
What needs to happen:
An acceptable piece of evidence is a threat-to-control matrix. 
This makes it much easier to see:
- which controls protect against multiple threats
- threats with inadequate protection
- duplicated controls
- especially important controls
- possible single points of security failure.
The outcome should not simply be "we have MFA", for example. The documentation should demonstrate which identified threats the control is intended to mitigate.

Action: Have you conducted a security design review against good practice principles and patterns?
What it means:
Has someone suitably knowledgeable stepped back and checked that the proposed security design is sensible, follows recognised good practice, and doesn't contain obvious architectural security weaknesses? This is slightly different from threat modelling.
Threat modelling asks how could this particular system be attacked or misused?”
A security design review asks, is the way we've designed the system fundamentally secure and consistent with accepted security principles?”
Why does this exist:
A team can identify individual threats and still end up with a poor overall security design.
For example, controls may exist but:
- be implemented in the wrong place
- rely too heavily on one component
- give users excessive privileges
- trust systems unnecessarily
- fail securely only in some circumstances
- produce inadequate security logs
- create unnecessarily complex security arrangements.
A design review provides another perspective on the overall security architecture.
Conditions:
The security design review should reflect the nature and risk of the service and consider relevant good-practice principles, including:
- least privilege and separation of duties
- defence in depth and secure-by-default design
- minimising the attack surface
- strong authentication and access controls
- appropriate encryption and secure credential management
- logging, monitoring and auditing
- resilience, secure failure and appropriate security boundaries
What needs to happen:
Complete and document a security design review using the current architecture, identified threats and proposed security controls. The review should:
- assess the design against recognised security principles and patterns
- identify any weaknesses, gaps or recommendations
- record actions and assign owners
- track significant issues through to resolution or formal risk acceptance
For higher-risk services, consider an independent or specialist security review.

Action: Do the scoring scales used for your service's security risk assessment align with your organisation's risk management processes?
What it means: Does the way you score security risks match the way your organisation scores and understands risk more generally?
Why does this exist:
Security risks ultimately need to be understood and managed alongside other organisational risks.
Using aligned scoring means:
- risks can be compared consistently
- senior decision-makers understand what the ratings mean
- escalation thresholds are consistent
- risks aren't understated or overstated because different teams use different definitions
- security risks can feed into wider organisational risk management.
Conditions: This applies wherever the service uses a scoring system to determine the likelihood, impact or overall severity of security risks.
What needs to happen:
- Identify the organisation's existing risk scoring framework.
- Use the same scales or establish a clear mapping between the security risk scale and organisational scale.
- Define what each likelihood, impact and severity rating means.
- Agree the scoring parameters with the appropriate risk/security stakeholders.
- Apply the scoring consistently across the service's security risks.

Action: Have you documented the risk assessment method used to perform a risk assessment?
What it means: Have you written down how you assess security risks so that someone can understand the process you followed and repeat it?
Why does this exist:
Risk assessments involve judgement. Without a defined method, two people could assess exactly the same risk and reach very different conclusions.
Documenting the method makes the assessment:
- consistent
- repeatable
- understandable
- auditable
- easier to review and update.
Conditions:
The documented method should cover the scope and approach to the assessment, including how threats, vulnerabilities, business impacts, likelihood and risk severity are identified and evaluated.
It should also define important terminology, assumptions and constraints. The guidance recommends documenting the assessment boundary and identifying what is in and out of scope.
What needs to happen:
Document the risk assessment methodology, including:
- scope and boundaries
- terminology and definitions
- assumptions and constraints
- information/sources used
- how threats, vulnerabilities and impacts are assessed
- how likelihood and impact are scored
- how the overall risk rating is calculated
- how and when risks will be reviewed.

Action: Have you validated the timeliness of the threat and business impact sources?
What it means: Have you checked that the information you're using to assess risk is still current enough to be relied upon?
Why does this exist:
A risk assessment is only as good as the information it is based on.
For example, a threat assessment could become outdated because new threats or attack techniques have emerged. Equally, an impact assessment could become outdated because the service now processes more sensitive information or serves significantly more users.
Using outdated information could result in the service underestimating or misrepresenting its actual security risk.
Conditions:
Check the age and relevance of information used to determine:
- threat actors and their capabilities
- threat likelihood
- vulnerabilities and attack techniques
- asset importance
- sensitivity of information
- number/type of users
- operational dependency on the service
- business consequences of compromise.
What needs to happen:
- Record the sources and dates of the threat and business-impact information used.
- Check that those sources are still relevant and current.
- Define when the information needs reviewing.
- Reassess it when significant changes occur to the service or threat landscape.
- Update the risk assessment where newer information changes likelihood or impact.

Action: Have you documented the service's risks (for example in a risk register)?
What it means: Have all the security risks you've identified been formally written down somewhere where they can be tracked, owned and managed?
Why does this exist:
Identifying a risk in a workshop or conversation isn't enough.
Risks need to be recorded so the organisation can understand:
- what could happen
- what could cause it
- what would be affected
- how serious it is
- who owns it
- what is being done about it
- whether the remaining risk is acceptable.
This also provides an audit trail for security and risk decisions.
Conditions:
Relevant identified security risks should be captured, including risks that have been accepted and those that are above the project's acceptable risk level and therefore require treatment.
The guidance recommends describing security risks in terms of the threat actor, threat event, vulnerability and resulting consequences.
What needs to happen: Create and maintain a risk register, it should be kept up to date, shared with the people responsible for decision-making and mitigation, and updated when controls are introduced or circumstances change. The guidance specifically describes the register as a "living document" and says scores should be updated following implementation of security controls to reflect the latest information.

Action: Have you identified the cyber security standards that are relevant to the service?
What it means: Have you worked out which recognised security standards, frameworks and guidance apply to the type of service you are building and the things it needs to protect?
Why does this exist:
Recognised standards and frameworks provide an established baseline of good security practice, rather than requiring each project to invent its own approach.
Using relevant standards helps teams:
- identify appropriate security protections
- avoid overlooking common security requirements
- manage vulnerabilities and risks consistently
- use a common security language
- support legal, regulatory and governance requirements.
Conditions:
The frameworks selected should reflect:
- what assets and information the service needs to protect
- the service's technical architecture and environment
- identified vulnerabilities and security risks
- whether it is cloud, SaaS, web, network-based, etc.
- applicable organisational, legal or regulatory security requirements.
The guidance says the service's assets, design, architecture and vulnerabilities should provide the basis for shortlisting appropriate security frameworks
What needs to happen:
- Identify what needs protecting.
- Review recognised standards and security frameworks.
- Decide which are relevant to the service and why.
- Document the standards/frameworks selected.
- Revisit them when the service or technology changes significantly.

Action: Have you agreed the security control frameworks you intend to use with your organisation’s security function?
What it means: Has your organisation's security team been involved in deciding and agreeing which security frameworks the service will use?
Why does this exist:
Your organisation may already have:
- required security frameworks
- standard security controls
- an organisational security controls taxonomy
- approved security patterns
- established security policies
- regulatory or compliance requirements.
Engaging the security function avoids individual services adopting inconsistent or unsuitable approaches and gives the project access to people who understand how the frameworks should be applied.
Conditions:
The selected frameworks should be appropriate to the assets, architecture, risks and technology of the service, while also meeting organisational security requirements.
The guidance says this activity should be led by technical and security architects in collaboration with security teams that understand security frameworks and how to interpret them
What needs to happen:
- Engage the organisation's security function.
- Identify any existing organisational security framework or controls taxonomy.
- Discuss which additional frameworks are relevant to the service.
- Agree which frameworks will provide the basis for the service's controls.
- Record that decision and make it available to the relevant delivery teams.

Action: Have you created a security controls set relevant to your service?
What it means: Have you turned the selected frameworks into a practical list of security controls that this particular service needs to implement?
Why does this exist:
Generic frameworks can contain many controls, not all of which will be relevant to every service.
Creating a service-specific controls set helps ensure that security measures are:
- appropriate to the service
- proportionate to its risks
- connected to what needs protecting
- understandable to delivery teams
- capable of being implemented and evidenced
- maintained as the service evolves.
Conditions:
The controls selected should take account of:
- service assets
- security risks and vulnerabilities
- technical architecture
- service environment
- applicable security obligations
- relevant security frameworks
- organisational security requirements.
If the standard frameworks do not address a particular security need, the guidance allows appropriate custom processes or controls to be added, with advice from the organisation's security professionals
What needs to happen:
Create and maintain a documented set of security controls specifically applicable to the service.
- what controls are required
- where the controls came from
- why they are relevant
- what part of the service they apply to
- how they relate to identified risks or requirements
- any service-specific/custom controls needed.
The controls set should also be shared with delivery teams and reviewed when significant functionality or components are added

Action: Does your security controls set map to the NCSC Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF)?
What it means: Can you show how the security controls selected for your service relate to the security outcomes in the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) Cyber Assessment Framework?
Why does this exist:
The CAF provides a common, outcome-focused way of looking at cyber security and resilience.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) describes CAF as a systematic approach to assessing how cyber risks are being managed. Its high-level objectives and principles are expressed as security outcomes rather than a simple checklist of individual technical measures.
Conditions:
The mapping should cover the service's relevant controls against applicable CAF outcomes.
CAF is structured around four high-level areas:
1. Managing security risk
2. Protecting against cyber attack
3. Detecting cyber security events
4. Minimising the impact of cyber security incidents
What needs to happen:
- Take the service's agreed security controls set.
- Map each relevant control to the corresponding CAF outcome/principle.
- Identify any CAF areas with insufficient control coverage.
- Address or explain gaps where appropriate.
- Maintain the mapping as the controls and service change.

Action: Have you treated the risks that have a rating above the project's risk appetite?
What it means: If any risks are larger than the level of risk the organisation is willing to accept, have you done something about them?
Why does this exist: Risk appetite defines how much security risk an organisation is prepared to tolerate. Risks that exceed this threshold cannot simply be ignored. Secure by Design states that risks should be reduced to an acceptable level through appropriate mitigations or approved acceptance decisions
Conditions:
Applies when:
- A security risk assessment has been completed.
- Risks have been scored.
- Some risks exceed agreed thresholds.
What needs to happen:
For every risk above tolerance, one of the following should occur:
- Reduce the risk through controls.
- Transfer the risk.
- Avoid the risk by changing the design.
- Escalate and formally accept the risk.
There should be clear evidence of the chosen approach.

Action: Have you documented the risk mitigations (for example in a risk treatment plan)?
What it means: Have you written down exactly what actions will be taken to reduce security risks?
Why does this exist: Mitigations that exist only in conversations are easily forgotten. A documented treatment plan provides accountability, allows progress to be tracked and demonstrates that risks are being managed systematically. Secure by Design recommends documenting and approving mitigation activities as part of risk management.
Conditions:
Applies when:
- Risks have been identified.
- Controls are needed.
- Risk responses have been agreed.
What needs to happen:
The documentation should show:
- The risk.
- Proposed mitigation.
- Owner.
- Due date.
- Current status.
- Expected reduction in risk.

Action: Did you select the security controls based on risk, threats and exposure?
What it means: Did you choose security controls because they address real threats and risks, rather than simply applying controls because they are standard or familiar?
Why does this exist: Secure by Design promotes a risk-driven approach. Controls should directly relate to the threats facing the service. Over-securing wastes money, while under-securing leaves vulnerabilities exposed
Conditions:
When:
- Threat assessments have been completed.
- Risks have been identified.
- Security architecture is being defined.
When:
- Threat assessments have been completed.
- Risks have been identified.
- Security architecture is being defined.
What needs to happen:
You should be able to demonstrate:
- Threats were identified.
- Risks were assessed.
- Controls were selected to reduce those specific risks.
- Control decisions can be traced back to identified risks.

Action: Have you documented the selected controls?
What it means: Have you recorded which security controls will be implemented and why?
Why does this exist: Without documentation there is no reliable evidence of what protections are expected, what has been implemented, or what auditors and assurance teams should verify. Secure by Design encourages use of security control frameworks and taxonomies to record selected controls
Conditions:
Applies when:
- Security controls have been identified.
- Solution design is underway.
- Assurance activities need traceability.
What needs to happen:
The documentation should include:
- Control name.
- Purpose.
- Associated risk.
- Owner.
- Implementation status.
- Relevant standards/framework references.

Action: Have you tested the controls and confirmed they're working as intended?
What it means: Have you checked that the security controls actually work in practice?
Why does this exist: A control that exists on paper may not work correctly. Secure by Design places emphasis on assessing the effectiveness of security controls and continuing assurance throughout delivery. A control only reduces risk if it operates as intended.
Conditions: When controls have been designed, built, configured and deployed.
What needs to happen:
Testing may include:
- Penetration testing.
- Vulnerability scanning.
- Security design reviews.
- Configuration reviews.
- User access testing.
- Red team exercises.
- Evidence-based assurance reviews.

Action: Have you identified any residual risks and raised them with risk owners for sign-off?
What it means: After all controls have been implemented, are there any risks that still remain, and have the people responsible formally agreed to accept them?
Why does this exist: No service is completely risk-free. Even after mitigation, some residual risk usually remains. Secure by Design requires accountability for those remaining risks, meaning appropriate risk owners must understand and formally accept them.
Conditions:
Applies when:
- Security controls have been implemented.
- Risks have been reassessed.
- Some level of risk remains.
What needs to happen:
You should:
1. Recalculate the risk after mitigation.
2. Identify remaining residual risks.
3. Record them in the risk register.
4. Present them to the appropriate risk owner.
5. Obtain formal acceptance or direction for further action.

Action: Do you have a documented approach on how to classify, prioritise and redress vulnerabilities?
What it means: Have you agreed and written down how you will judge how serious a vulnerability is, decide which ones need fixing first, and determine how and when they will be fixed?
Why does this exist:
Not every vulnerability presents the same level of risk. A minor weakness in a low-risk component should not necessarily receive the same priority as a critical vulnerability affecting an important internet-facing system.
Having an agreed process ensures vulnerabilities are handled consistently and that teams focus first on weaknesses presenting the greatest risk.
Conditions: Different vulnerabilities may require different responses. The guidance gives examples including patches or updates, compensating controls, code fixes and workarounds, with more serious issues potentially requiring senior-management escalation
What needs to happen:
Create and maintain a documented vulnerability management process that defines:
- how vulnerabilities are classified and scored
- how priority is determined
- expected remediation timescales
- available remediation approaches
- who is responsible for resolving them
- when vulnerabilities need escalating
- how remediation is tested and confirmed
- how vulnerabilities are recorded and tracked.

Action: Do you have a documented process for identifying and responding to new vulnerabilities in your code, systems or supply chain?
What it means: Do you have an ongoing way of finding out when new security weaknesses affect your service and a clear process for deciding what to do when one is discovered?
Why does this exist: A service may be secure today but become vulnerable tomorrow because a new weakness is discovered in software or a dependency it uses.
Conditions:
The process should cover vulnerabilities discovered through sources such as:
- vulnerability scanning
- security testing
- automated dependency tools
- supplier/vendor notifications
- vulnerability or threat alerts
- penetration tests
- internal reporting
- external vulnerability reports.
What needs to happen:
Document how the team will:
1. monitor for new vulnerabilities
2. determine whether the service is affected
3. record the vulnerability
4. assess its severity and impact
5. notify or escalate it to the appropriate people
6. assign remediation work
7. patch, fix or mitigate it
8. test that the action worked
9. update the vulnerability register.

Action: Are you following a secure systems software development life cycle policy or process?
What it means: Is security built into the way the service is designed, developed, tested, deployed and maintained, rather than being checked only at the end?
Why does this exist:
Security problems are generally easier to address when they are identified as part of normal development rather than after the service is complete or live.
A secure development lifecycle encourages teams to consider security while, Designing 
Building
Reviewing
Testing 
Deploying 
Operating
rather than relying solely on a final security assessment.
Conditions:
The appropriate process will depend on the service, but should incorporate relevant security activities throughout development, such as:
- threat modelling
- secure design
- code review
- automated security testing
- dependency checking
- vulnerability scanning
- remediation
- appropriate security testing before deployment.
What needs to happen:
- Have an agreed secure development lifecycle or development process.
- Define the security activities required at appropriate development stages.
- Build appropriate security checks into development and deployment workflows.
- Define who is responsible for completing those checks.
- Record and address vulnerabilities discovered.
- Continue security testing after the service goes live.

Action: Are you conducting regular code reviews as part of the development process?
What it means: Does another suitably experienced person review code changes before they are accepted or deployed?
Why does this exist:
Developers can unintentionally introduce:
- security weaknesses
- coding errors
- insecure configurations
- unintended behaviour
- problems created by changes elsewhere in the system.
Conditions:
Code reviews should form part of the development/change process and should be performed by someone suitably experienced who did not submit the relevant change.
The extent of review can be proportionate to the nature and risk of the change. Platform rules and review checklists can also be used to make the process consistent
What needs to happen:
- Define when code review is required.
- Require an appropriate independent reviewer.
- Prevent relevant changes from being merged/deployed until required reviews are complete.
- Include security considerations in review criteria where appropriate.
- Maintain evidence that reviews occurred.
- Address issues identified before release.

Action: Are you using a manual or automated code testing method (for example, Static Application Security Testing (SAST) or Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST))?
What it means: Are you actively testing the application for security weaknesses using appropriate security testing techniques or tools?
Why does this exist:
Human code review alone may not detect every vulnerability.
Automated and manual security testing provides additional layers of assurance and can identify vulnerabilities earlier and more consistently.
The guidance recommends multiple methods rather than relying on one vulnerability-discovery process.
Conditions:
The testing methods should be:
- suitable for the technology being used
- proportionate to relevant threats and risk
- run at appropriate points in development
- repeated at suitable frequencies
- capable of feeding findings to the people responsible for remediation.
The guidance distinguishes between continual tests, periodic tests and tests triggered by events such as deployment or the integration of new third-party software
What needs to happen:
- Select appropriate code/application security testing methods.
- Integrate automated testing into development pipelines where appropriate.
- Define when tests will run.
- Configure alerts/reporting so developers see important findings.
- Record identified vulnerabilities.
- Prioritise and remediate findings using the vulnerability management process.
- Retest where appropriate to confirm remediation.

Action: Do you have a plan for carrying out penetration tests with appropriate scopes?
What it means: Have you planned when penetration testing will happen and clearly defined what the testers are supposed to test and what the test is intended to prove?
Why does this exist:
A penetration test is much more useful when it is targeted at the relevant risks and parts of the service.
A poorly scoped test could miss important systems or attack paths, while testing against a realistic threat scenario can provide assurance about whether the service's protections work as expected. The guidance emphasises that penetration testing is primarily a means of gaining assurance in security and vulnerability-management processes, rather than being the organisation's sole method for identifying vulnerabilities.
Conditions:
Planning should consider:
- what systems/applications are being tested
- the objective of the test
- relevant threat scenarios
- what is in and out of scope
- the appropriate timing
- who will undertake the test
- how results will be reported and managed.
The frequency should reflect the threats and risk involved, and vulnerability testing may also need to be triggered by significant service changes or new third-party components
What needs to happen:
Create a documented penetration-testing plan that establishes:
- purpose: what assurance the test should provide
- scope: applications, infrastructure, APIs or other components included
- boundaries: what's specifically excluded
- threat scenarios: what realistic risks the test should examine
- timing/frequency: when testing will happen
- responsibility: who will commission and perform it
- reporting: how findings will be recorded and communicated
- remediation: how identified vulnerabilities will be prioritised, assigned and fixed.
Guidance:
https://www.security.gov.uk/policy-and-guidance/secure-by-design/activities/discovering-vulnerabilities/

Procuring external IT security assurance expertise, including SIRAs and ITHCs

Action: Do you have a documented approach for what events should be logged to help identify security incidents?
What it means: Have you decided and written down which activities and events within the service need to be recorded so that suspicious behaviour or a security incident can be detected and investigated?
Why does this exist:
If important events are not recorded, you may not know that an attack or security incident has happened.
Appropriate logging allows teams to:
- spot unusual or suspicious behaviour
- investigate potential security incidents
- understand what happened and when
- provide information to incident response teams
- monitor whether security controls are working
- identify opportunities to improve security.
Conditions: The events you log should reflect the service's architecture, assets, threats and risks. The guidance specifically recommends using the threat assessment, threat model and security risk mitigations to help determine what information could be useful during an incident.
What needs to happen:
- Identify the security events and information that need to be captured.
- Link them to relevant service assets, risks and threats.
- Document what will be logged and why.
- Make sure appropriate systems/components generate the required information.
- Secure the logs against unauthorised access, alteration or deletion.
- Define suitable retention arrangements.
- Review logging requirements when the service or threat landscape changes.

Action: Have you determined the tools required to log and analyse the event logs and trigger alerts?
What it means: Have you worked out what technology is needed to collect security information, analyse it and notify the right people when something suspicious happens?
Why does this exist:
A service could generate millions of log entries. It may be unrealistic for people to manually read those records looking for suspicious activity.
Appropriate tools help teams:
- bring relevant security information together
- search and analyse events
- identify patterns or anomalies
- generate alerts when defined conditions occur
- provide information to security or incident-response teams.
The guidance recommends investigating whether appropriate capabilities exist to collect and monitor observables and identifying additional capabilities needed to provide sufficient visibility.
Conditions:
The tools should reflect:
- the type and volume of information produced
- identified security threats
- service architecture
- monitoring requirements
- organisational security capabilities
- incident-response arrangements
- third-party services.
Where third-party suppliers provide service components, their monitoring, logging and alerting capabilities should also be considered.
What needs to happen:
'- Identify what logs and security information need collecting.
- Determine which existing organisational tools can be used.
- Identify any additional monitoring capability required.
- Configure tools to collect and securely store the required information.
- Configure appropriate alerts.
- Ensure information can be searched and analysed.
- Integrate with the DfE's Security Operations Centre (SOC) or incident-response capabilities where appropriate.

Action: Do you have a documented approach for analysing your logs and monitoring the alerts generated?
What it means: Do you have a documented approach for analysing your logs and monitoring the alerts generated?
Why does this exist:
An alert only protects the service if something appropriate happens as a result.
A documented monitoring process helps ensure that:
- alerts are seen by the right people
- genuine incidents are identified
- false positives can be investigated
- serious events are escalated quickly
- incident management processes are triggered where necessary
- responsibilities are clear.
Conditions:
The approach should reflect the importance and urgency of different events.
For example, some information might simply require periodic review, while more serious events might require immediate alerts or automated action. The guidance recommends applying appropriate actions to each observable and incorporating observability into the threat model
What needs to happen:
Document:
- which logs and alerts will be monitored
- who is responsible for monitoring them
- how frequently they are reviewed
- which events require investigation
- when an alert should be generated
- how alerts are prioritised
- who receives alerts
- when an incident should be escalated
- what automated responses exist, where appropriate
- how monitoring feeds into incident management.
The process should be reviewed when the service or threats change.

Action: Does the service delivery change management process consider the impact of changes to security?
What it means: Whenever someone proposes a change to the service, is security considered before that change is approved and released?
Why does this exist:
A service that is secure today may become less secure after a change.
Changes can introduce:
- vulnerabilities
- new attack routes
- insecure configurations
- changes to data exposure
- weakened security controls
- new dependencies.
The guidance states that changes can affect the service's security posture regardless of whether they are relatively small technical modifications or major changes to the service design.
Conditions:
Security impact should be considered for service changes, particularly those affecting areas such as:
- applications or operating systems
- infrastructure
- ports, protocols or services
- hardware platforms
- processing, storage or transmission of information
- identity and access management
- cryptography
- security/privacy controls
- third-party services
- procedures that could create opportunities for misuse or fraud.
What needs to happen:
Build security checks into the change-management process so that:
- the scope and purpose of the change are documented
- affected systems, components and data are identified
- security impacts are assessed
- impacts on existing security controls are considered
- additional controls are identified where necessary
- appropriate security testing takes place before release
- the outcome is recorded within the change-management tooling.
Guidance:
https://www.security.gov.uk/policy-and-guidance/secure-by-design/activities/evaluating-the-security-impact-of-changes/

How do I? - Change Enablement Policy Process and Procedure v1.05 - MyDfE

Action: Are you reflecting requested changes in the service’s threat model?
What it means: When the service changes, do you check whether that change introduces new threats or attack routes and update the threat model where necessary?
Why does this exist:
A threat model represents the security threats relevant to a particular design.
If the design changes but the threat model does not, the model may no longer accurately describe the risks facing the service.
Keeping it updated also ensures security controls remain appropriate to the current service rather than an earlier version of it.
Conditions:
Changes should be assessed to determine whether they affect:
- service architecture
- attack surface
- data flows
- trust boundaries
- users or access
- external integrations
- vulnerabilities
- existing attack paths
- existing security controls.
Where the change does not materially affect threats, record that conclusion. Where it does, update the relevant threat documentation.
What needs to happen:
- Review proposed changes for security implications.
- Determine whether threats or attack paths have changed.
- Add new threats where appropriate.
- Update existing threats where their likelihood or impact has changed.
- Identify any additional security controls required.
- Keep the threat model aligned with the latest service design.
Guidance:
https://www.security.gov.uk/policy-and-guidance/secure-by-design/activities/evaluating-the-security-impact-of-changes/

How do I? - Change Enablement Policy Process and Procedure v1.05 - MyDfE

Action: Are you considering requested changes as part of risk assessment and treatment activities?
What it means: When something changes in the service, do you check whether it creates new security risks or changes existing ones, and do you decide what action is required?
Why does this exist:
A change could:
- create a completely new risk
- increase an existing risk
- reduce an existing risk
- make a security control less effective
- require an additional security control.
Risk assessment therefore needs to remain aligned with the current service.
Conditions:
Consider whether the change affects:
- threats or vulnerabilities
- likelihood of an incident
- potential business impact
- attack surface
- existing risk ratings
- effectiveness of existing controls
- need for additional controls.
The depth of reassessment should be proportionate to the security significance of the change
What needs to happen:
For relevant changes:
1. assess the security impact
2. review affected risks
3. identify new risks where needed
4. reassess likelihood and impact where appropriate
5. update the risk register
6. review whether existing mitigations remain effective
7. identify additional controls or mitigations if required
8. test security recommendations before release.
Guidance:
https://www.security.gov.uk/policy-and-guidance/secure-by-design/activities/evaluating-the-security-impact-of-changes/

How do I? - Change Enablement Policy Process and Procedure v1.05 - MyDfE

Action: Are you appropriately escalating any changes that create risks above the project's risk appetite?
What it means: If a proposed change creates a security risk that is greater than the level the project is authorised to accept, is that risk being raised with someone who has the authority to decide what happens?
Why does this exist:
Some security decisions are bigger than the delivery team's authority.
If a change creates an unacceptable risk, an appropriate decision-maker may need to determine whether to:
- introduce additional controls
- modify the change
- delay the change
- not proceed
- accept the residual risk where they have authority to do so.
This preserves accountability for significant security-risk decisions and prevents unacceptable risks being accepted informally as part of routine delivery.
Conditions:
This applies where the security assessment of a proposed change identifies new or increased security risk,  risk is assessed, resulting rating exceeds the project's agreed risk appetite.
The change-management process should therefore connect to the project's wider risk-management and governance arrangements.
What needs to happen:
- Assess the security risk associated with relevant changes.
- Compare the resulting risk rating with the project's risk appetite.
- Identify additional mitigations where possible.
- Escalate risks above appetite to the appropriate risk owner or decision-maker.
- Record the decision and any conditions or actions.
- Do not treat significant risk acceptance as an informal delivery-team decision.
- Update the risk register and treatment actions accordingly.

Action: Have you identified components to be retired in the asset inventory?
What it means: Have you clearly identified and recorded which parts of the service are going to be switched off, removed, replaced or decommissioned?
Why does this exist:
You cannot safely retire something unless you understand what it is, what information it contains and what relies upon it.
For example, simply switching off an application could leave behind:
- cloud infrastructure that is still publicly accessible
- unused accounts or credentials
- databases containing sensitive information
- domains that are no longer managed
- integrations pointing at systems that no longer exist
- forgotten test or pre-production environments.
Conditions:
This rule applies whenever an asset or component is:
- no longer required
- being replaced
- reaching end of life
- being removed following a service change
- affected by the end of a supplier contract
- left over from a pilot or trial
- being retired as part of shutting down the entire service.
Connected assets and dependencies also need to be considered, not just the main component being retired
What needs to happen:
- Maintain an up-to-date inventory of service assets.
- Clearly identify the components scheduled for retirement.
- Identify the asset owner.
- Record what data the component holds or processes.
- Identify dependent or connected systems.
- Involve the relevant asset owners in retirement planning.
- After retirement, update the asset inventory to show that the component is no longer active.

Action: Have you conducted a retirement risk assessment with an appropriate plan put together based on the classification and sensitivity of data?
What it means: Before switching something off or getting rid of it, have you assessed what could go wrong and created a plan for safely dealing with the systems and data involved?
Why does this exist:
Retiring a component can itself introduce security risks.
For example:
- sensitive data could inadvertently remain behind
- information that legally needs retaining could be accidentally destroyed
- necessary data could become inaccessible
- a connected service could stop working
- old infrastructure could remain accessible
- user/admin access could remain active
- data could be inadequately deleted and later recovered.
Conditions:
The assessment should consider:
- the classification and sensitivity of the data
- data-retention requirements
- whether data needs to be archived, migrated or deleted
- regulatory or contractual requirements
- backups
- dependencies on other systems
- effects on connected services
- temporary risks during the retirement process
- remaining infrastructure, accounts and access
- residual risks following retirement.
The required disposal method should be proportionate to the sensitivity of the information. guidance specifically notes that simply deleting files may not prevent recovery of data and recommends sanitisation where storage media has contained data sensitive to the organisation
What needs to happen: Conduct and document a retirement risk assessment and use it to create a retirement/decommissioning plan. Where backups must be retained, the guidance says they should continue to receive appropriate security protection and should be tested to ensure required information can actually be restored

Action: Have you included security considerations within a formal closeout report to be shared with relevant stakeholders?
What it means: Once the component or service has been retired, have you formally documented what was done, confirmed that the security actions were completed, recorded anything still outstanding, and shared that information with the appropriate people?
Why does this exist:
A retirement project should not simply finish when a system is switched off.
There needs to be confidence that:
- components were actually decommissioned
- access was removed
- information was appropriately migrated or destroyed
- infrastructure was removed
- relevant records were updated
- outstanding security risks were identified
- someone remains responsible for those risks.
The closeout report creates an audit trail and provides senior stakeholders with assurance that decommissioning was completed safely
Conditions: The report should reflect the actual outcome of the retirement activity. This becomes particularly important if the project or delivery team itself is being closed, because any remaining responsibilities and risks need to be transferred rather than becoming ownerless. The guidance notes that senior responsible owners, service owners and product managers should be kept informed, and that the CISO or CDIO may need involvement where responsible project roles are being wound down
What needs to happen:
Create a formal closeout report confirming:
- what was retired
- what security actions were completed
- how relevant data was handled
- whether access and infrastructure were removed
- whether asset records have been updated
- any outstanding actions
- any residual risks
- recommendations or follow-up activity
- who owns any remaining risks or responsibilities.
Share the report with the relevant stakeholders and decision-makers.
